facts: Everything Is F*cked: A Book About Hope opens with Witold Pilecki, a Polish officer who in 1940 had himself sent to Auschwitz.
On 19 September 1940 he stood in a Warsaw street roundup of about 2,000 men. He reached Auschwitz on 21-22 September with 1,705 others, as prisoner 4859 under the name Tomasz Serafinski.
Inside he built an underground group and a homemade radio transmitter, finished over seven months, that sent arrival and death figures until autumn 1942. He sent secret reports from October 1940.
He escaped on the night of 26-27 April 1943 and wrote a report that August. The communist-run Polish state executed him on 25 May 1948.
Manson reads Pilecki as heroism, the ability to conjure hope where none exists, and uses him to ask where hope comes from.
Manson defines hope as the belief that you can make progress toward something valuable, resting on a sense of control, belief in the value of something and community.
The book ends by asking the reader to act without hope: to not hope for better, to be better.

ZOW worked in cells of five and aimed to raise morale, bring news, share food and clothing, build intelligence and prepare to seize the camp if a relief attack came; his reports were a principal Auschwitz intelligence source for the Western Allies.

He escaped with two comrades after the camp Gestapo had killed many ZOW members, hoping to persuade the Home Army to attempt a rescue; the Home Army judged a rescue attack would fail for lack of transport, supplies and shelter.
scene_details: A Warsaw street roundup in September 1940
A radio transmitter built over seven months inside the camp
tension: A man chose a place with no visible hope and built something there anyway.
opening_idea: Start with Pilecki standing in the Warsaw roundup, or with the number 4859.

lessons.idea: Hope holds up when it is tied to a task you can still move, however small.
lessons.anchor: Pilecki's radio, built over seven months, was something he could do inside the camp.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: An employee on a failing team who takes one fixable process in hand.

reflect_final: In a situation that feels stuck right now, what is one thing within reach that you could build slowly?

use_cases.situation: Your team feels the project is doomed.
use_cases.move: Mention the radio Pilecki built over seven months and ask which small piece is still in your hands.

use_cases.situation: A friend says nothing they do matters.
use_cases.move: Ask what they could finish this week that would still be there next month.

use_cases.situation: You feel hopeless about a long problem.
use_cases.move: Name the one part you control and put it on the calendar.

pocket_idea: Pilecki built a radio inside Auschwitz over seven months: hope stays alive on the part you can still move.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Pilecki had himself arrested in Warsaw so he could build a resistance inside Auschwitz.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Pilecki joins a 1940 Warsaw roundup, enters Auschwitz as 4859, builds an underground network and a radio, escapes in 1943; Manson opens his hope book with him.
